title: If any image deserved honor, the bronze serpent did—yet incense alone brought it down; Nicaea II’s lights clash with that
source_text: XLVI. Nam si unquam extitit imago, quae venerationem aliquam mereretur, procul dubio fuit ille serpens. Nam expresso Dei mandato Moses vir tantus illum fabricaverat. Instrumentum fuerat insignis admodum liberationis, Israelitis in deserto concessae, & memoriam ejus in populo isto conservabat; ac denique eximius erat Christi olim venturi, & in crucem tollendi typus. Et tamen Ezechias, Deo instigante, non solum prohibuit ne Judaei illum colerent; sed propter istud tantum, quod filii Israel adolebant ei incensum, indignabundus illum confregit atque comminuit. Quomodo ergo cum Dei voluntate congruit quod sanxit Synodus Nicena secunda, scilicet, ad imagines reverenter accedendum esse oblationibus suffituum, atque luminarium? Et quantula pars est honoris, qui Christi & Sanctorum imaginibus defertur, in Ecclesia Romana, Thuris accensio, atque oblatio?
pass_a_gloss: For if ever there existed an image which merited some veneration, without doubt it was that serpent. For by the express commandment of God Moses, so great a man, had fabricated it. It had been the instrument of a liberation altogether signal, granted to the Israelites in the desert, and it conserved the memory of that in that people; and finally it was an outstanding type of Christ once to come, and to be lifted up on the cross. And yet Hezekiah, God instigating, not only prohibited that the Jews cultivate it; but for that alone, that the children of Israel burned incense to it, indignant broke it and shattered it. How then does it agree with the will of God what the second Nicene Synod sanctioned, namely, that one must approach images reverently with offerings of incense, and of lights? And how small a part is the kindling and offering of frankincense of the honor which is paid to the images of Christ and of the Saints in the Roman Church?
pass_b_english: Bronze serpent had divine mandate, saving use, memorial force, and Christ-typology—best-case image.
Incense alone justified smashing it; Nicaea II’s incense-and-lights approach collides with that verdict.
